definition.text: In economics, land means every naturally occurring resource, not just the ground itself.

facts.text: Examples include particular locations, mineral deposits, forests, fish stocks, air quality, geostationary orbits and parts of the electromagnetic spectrum.
Land is one of the three classic factors of production, alongside capital and labour.
Natural resources underlie the production of every good, including capital goods.
Income earned from owning or controlling natural resources is called rent.
Land's role was argued over at length in classical economics but became minor in 20th-century neoclassical economics.
In the UK, the non-produced asset of land makes up 51% of the country's total net worth.
Because nobody created land, it has no original owner, and rival claims to locations and mineral deposits have fed many civil wars and revolutions.
Richard T. Ely, founder of the American Economic Association, established it in 1925.

definition.text: Capital means durable goods that people have produced and then use to make further goods and services.

facts.text: A typical example is the machinery in a factory.
Unlike raw materials or energy, capital is not used up in one round of production but gives productive services over many cycles.
Economists treat capital as a factor of production alongside labour and land, a classification dating from classical economics.
Unlike land and non-renewable resources, capital can be produced or increased.
A nation's capital stock includes buildings, equipment, software and inventories, and modern usage also counts non-physical assets.
Capital goods are bought to make other goods, while consumer goods are bought to be consumed: a chocolate bar is a consumer good, the machine that makes it is capital.
Investment, or capital accumulation, means producing goods that are not consumed straight away but used to produce other goods.

definition.text: Economists divide capital into several kinds, including financial, social, instructional, human, public and natural capital.

facts.text: Financial capital is traded in financial markets, and its market value rests on expected revenues and risk rather than on money invested in the past.
Human capital broadly combines social, instructional and individual human talent.
Public capital covers government-owned infrastructure such as highways, water treatment, electric grids, hospitals and schools.
Natural capital is the world's stock of natural resources, and some of it gives people free goods and services called ecosystem services.

definition.text: Adam Smith split capital into fixed capital, which is not used up in making a product, and circulating capital, which is.

facts.text: Machines and storage buildings are fixed capital, while raw materials and intermediate products are circulating capital.
Smith also made clear that capital is a stock.
In Marx's theory, constant capital is spending on machinery and plant, while variable capital is spending on labour power, which he saw as the only source of surplus value.

definition.text: Factors of production are the inputs used to make goods and services, such as land, labour and capital.

facts.text: How much of each input is used determines output through a relationship called the production function.
One common list names four basic factors: land, labour, capital and the entrepreneur.
Land, labour and capital are primary factors; materials and energy are secondary because they come from the primary ones.
Primary factors help production without becoming part of the product or being much changed by it.
Adam Smith and David Ricardo saw the parts of a price as payments for land (rent), labour (wages) and capital.
The 18th-century French physiocrats held that a nation's wealth came only from land and agriculture.
Some economists, such as Robert Ayres and Benjamin Warr, fault orthodox economics for overlooking natural resources and declining resource capital.

title: Ecological factors of production

definition.text: Ecological economics replaces the usual factors of production with matter, energy and design intelligence, so that production obeys physical limits.

facts.text: Matter can be recycled but not created or destroyed, so there is an upper limit on how much material can be withdrawn and used.
Energy loses usefulness over time through entropy, as when electricity running a machine turns into heat.
At the maximum sustainable rates of matter and energy use, only better design can raise productivity.
This underlies a core claim of ecological economics: infinite growth is impossible.

distinct_from: Entrepreneurship as a factor of production

title: Entrepreneurship as a factor of production

definition.text: Entrepreneurship, the organising work of combining land, labour and capital to make a profit, is sometimes counted as a fourth factor of production.

facts.text: Some authors added it in the first half of the 20th century, and it became standard in the post-war neoclassical synthesis.
Many economists today instead treat human capital as the fourth factor, with entrepreneurship as a form of it.
Others have proposed energy, social capital or cultural heritage as additional factors.

definition.text: An incentive is anything that persuades a person or organisation to change their behaviour toward a desired outcome.

facts.text: Disincentives work the other way, discouraging certain actions.
Governments, businesses and other organisations commonly use incentives to encourage particular behaviour.
Incentives are often split into intrinsic ones, driven by personal interest or enjoyment, and extrinsic ones, such as pay, recognition or the threat of punishment.
One scheme sorts incentives into financial (material rewards), moral (doing what is seen as right) and coercive (threat of force).
A misaligned incentive arises when parties' goals conflict, which happens in firms and also in environmental policy.
Incentives can produce unintended outcomes.
A 2026 meta-analysis of 2,193 estimates from 88 experiments found that financial incentives have a mean effect on performance close to zero in most field settings.

definition.text: Marginal utility is the extra satisfaction a person gets from consuming one more unit of a good or service.

facts.text: In economics, marginal means a small change from some starting level, such as the benefit of the next piece of chocolate.
Marginal utility can be positive, negative or zero; negative means each extra unit does more harm than good.
Marginal analysis compares the extra benefits of an activity with its extra costs.
Because utility is hard to measure directly, economists use revealed preferences, ranking options by watching what people choose.
Economists developed the idea of marginal utility while trying to explain how prices are set.
Daniel Bernoulli published the first clear statement of the theory in 1738.
Critics note that people may not optimise as the theory assumes, and that utility varies between people and over time.

title: Diminishing marginal utility
article: Marginal utility#Law of diminishing marginal utility

definition.text: The law of diminishing marginal utility says that each extra unit of something consumed adds less satisfaction than the one before.

facts.text: Three pieces of candy beat two, but the twentieth adds little beyond the nineteenth and may even make things worse.
The principle is reflected in the concave shape of most utility functions.
It helps explain things such as time preference and the value of goods.
Bernoulli and Cramer concluded that money becomes less desirable as more of it accumulates.
Risk aversion is mainly attributed to decreasing marginal utility.

definition.text: The Marginal Revolution was the spread of marginal utility theory in the 1870s through the work of Jevons in England, Menger in Austria and Walras in Switzerland.

facts.text: Jevons argued that value depends entirely on utility, publishing The Theory of Political Economy in 1871.
Carl Menger presented the theory in his Principles of Economics in 1871, and Walras in 1874.
A second generation, including Alfred Marshall, Böhm-Bawerk, Wieser and Pareto, carried the ideas into the mainstream.
Over the 20th century a large literature grew on the conflict between marginalism and the labour theory of value.

definition.text: The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the best alternative you give up when limited resources force you to pick one option over others.

facts.text: It is the benefit you would have had from the second-best choice.
Opportunity cost expresses the link between scarcity and choice, and its aim is efficient use of scarce resources.
It counts all costs of a decision, both explicit and implicit, and is not limited to money: lost time, pleasure or any useful benefit also counts.
If someone leaves work for an hour to spend $200 on office supplies and earns $25 an hour, the $200 is the explicit cost and the $25 of lost earnings the implicit cost.
Sunk costs, already spent and unrecoverable, are excluded and should not sway present or future decisions.
A party that can produce something at a lower opportunity cost than others has a comparative advantage in it.
Governments face opportunity costs too: $840 billion spent on a war cannot fund healthcare, education or tax cuts.

definition.text: An explicit cost is a direct, out-of-pocket cost of an action, paid in cash or by handing over resources.

facts.text: Explicit costs always have a money value and involve a transfer of money, such as paying employees.
Examples include wages, rent, overheads and materials.
They show up in a firm's financial statements, unlike implicit costs, which are hidden and not recorded in accounts.

title: Economic profit
article: Opportunity cost#Economic profit versus accounting profit

definition.text: Economic profit is revenue minus all costs including opportunity costs, whereas accounting profit counts only the measurable costs of running a business.

facts.text: In one example, starting a business gives $10,000 of accounting profit but −$30,000 of economic profit, because the opportunity costs outweigh the gain.
When economic profit is zero, revenue covers all explicit and implicit costs and there is no reason to move resources elsewhere; this is called normal profit.
Economic profit does not show whether a decision makes money, but whether it is wiser than the alternatives.

title: Rational choice model

definition.text: Rational choice modelling explains economic and social behaviour by imagining how a rational person would act when weighing the same costs and benefits.

facts.text: It assumes people have preferences among options that can be ranked and weighed, so they choose by balancing costs and benefits.
Preferences are assumed to be complete and transitive, and a decision counts as rational if it follows logically from them.
Early neoclassical economists such as Jevons assumed people choose to maximise their happiness, or utility.
It can explain how individually rational people reach collectively irrational outcomes.
Herbert Simon's bounded rationality suggests people often settle for a good-enough decision, which he called satisficing.
Behavioural psychology research has challenged the theory, giving rise to prospect theory as an alternative.
Critics also argue that people often act from habit, impulse or emotion rather than calculation.

contested_note: Economists, psychologists and sociologists have long disputed both the assumptions and the predictions of rational choice theory.

definition.text: A trade-off is a choice in which you accept less of one thing in return for more of another.

facts.text: Trade-offs arise from limits of many kinds, even simple physics: a full container must lose some items before it can take more.
In economics a trade-off is expressed as the opportunity cost of a choice, the most preferred alternative given up.
Investing in stocks offers higher potential returns with more risk, while bonds are safer but pay less.
Economists often draw trade-offs as a Pareto frontier, such as the production possibilities frontier between two goods.
In environmental management, REDD+ funding faces trade-offs among biodiversity conservation, carbon storage and fair distribution, since maximising one reduces the other two.
Tension between prosperity for all and environmental conservation makes trade-offs necessary in sustainability.

title: Utility

definition.text: In economics, utility is a measure of how satisfied a person is with a particular state of the world.

facts.text: Normatively, utility is a goal to maximise, close to the utilitarian idea of Bentham and Mill; descriptively, it is what people's choices reveal they are pursuing.
A utility function gives each option a number so that preferred options always get higher numbers.
Because utility cannot be observed directly, economists infer it from choices, for example from willingness to pay; Paul Samuelson called these revealed preferences.
Economists separate total utility, the utility of a whole bundle, from marginal utility, the change from one more unit of a good.
Indifference curves plot combinations of goods that give the same satisfaction, and combined with a budget constraint they yield demand curves.
Joan Robinson called utility circular: goods have utility because people want them, and people wanting them shows they have utility.

contested_note: Economists and ethicists disagree about how the normative and descriptive meanings of utility relate, and critics such as Joan Robinson call the concept circular.

title: Cardinal utility

definition.text: Cardinal utility treats satisfaction as something that can be measured with numbers, so the size of the differences between options means something.

facts.text: Utility functions are cardinal or ordinal depending on whether they say anything beyond the ranking of options, such as how strong a preference is.
Ordinal utility only ranks options: it can say two ice creams beat one, but not by how much.
Daniel Bernoulli used a logarithmic cardinal utility of money to resolve the St. Petersburg paradox.
It seems to assume absolute levels of satisfaction exist, so gains in satisfaction can be compared across situations.

definition.text: A budget constraint is the full set of combinations of goods and services a person can afford with their income at current prices.

facts.text: With two goods it is a straight line, the budget line, showing the trade-off between them.
The slope of the budget line is the price ratio of the two goods, which is the opportunity cost of one more unit of one good in units of the other.
Together with indifference curves, the budget constraint is the basic tool for analysing consumer choice.
The best affordable bundle usually lies where an indifference curve just touches the budget line.
Taxes, subsidies, quantity discounts and welfare benefits can make budget constraints kinked or non-linear.
In labour economics, the wage acts as the price of leisure: one more hour of leisure costs one hour's wage.

definition.text: An intertemporal budget constraint links what a person can consume in different periods through borrowing and saving at an interest rate.

facts.text: Borrowing now raises present consumption at the cost of less consumption later, while saving does the reverse.
Behavioural economics adds present bias, in which people give extra weight to consumption now over consumption later.

definition.text: A soft budget constraint exists when an organisation expects an outside body, usually a government, to cover its losses if it gets into financial trouble.

facts.text: Hungarian economist János Kornai introduced the term in the late 1970s to study state-owned firms in centrally planned economies.
Expecting bailouts, such firms invested too much, saved too little on costs and lobbied for more resources, contributing to chronic shortages.
The expectation of rescue creates moral hazard, as with too-big-to-fail banks.

definition.text: Ceteris paribus is a Latin phrase meaning 'other things being equal', used to study the effect of one change while assuming everything else stays the same.

facts.text: A standard example: if the price of milk falls, ceteris paribus, people will buy more milk.
The clause does not claim nothing else changes; it isolates the effect of one change.
Alfred Marshall popularised it in the 19th century, describing it as a 'pound' where disturbing causes are set aside for a time.
Because economic variables can only be isolated in theory, ceteris paribus can only reveal tendencies, not absolutes.
Marshall warned that the narrower the question, the less closely it matches real life, as in assuming hydrocarbon fuels are infinite.
In highly interconnected systems, changing one variable changes all the others, so holding everything else constant is not possible in reality.

title: Comparative advantage

definition.text: Comparative advantage is the principle that people, firms and countries can gain from trade even when one of them is better at producing everything.

facts.text: Gains are greatest when each party specialises in what it produces at the lowest opportunity cost and trades for the rest.
It differs from absolute advantage, which is about being more productive overall.
David Ricardo developed the classical theory in 1817, using the example of Portugal and England producing wine and cloth.
Ricardo's theory emerged in the debate over Britain's 1815 Corn Laws, which taxed imported grain to protect landowners.
In 1930 Gottfried Haberler restated the idea in terms of opportunity cost, measuring a good's value in forgone units of another good.
It describes the benefits specialisation and trade would bring, not a strict prediction of actual behaviour.
Critics such as James K. Galbraith argue that countries locked into agriculture stay poor because farming depends on land, a finite resource.

contested_note: Some economists dispute that comparative advantage justifies free trade, pointing to strategic trade policy and global value chains.

definition.text: Compensating variation is the amount of money that would leave a person exactly as well off after a price change as before, measured at the new prices.

facts.text: John Hicks introduced the measure in 1939.
It can be read as what a planner must pay to compensate a consumer for a price change after it happens.
It underlies Kaldor–Hicks efficiency: a policy passes if winners could compensate losers, even if they do not.
When a price change has no income effect, compensating variation equals equivalent variation and both equal the change in consumer surplus.

definition.text: Complementary goods are goods used together, so that one becomes more attractive as the other becomes more popular.

facts.text: Demand for a complement rises when the price of the other good falls, giving a negative cross elasticity of demand.
Cars and petrol, phones and phone service, and printers and cartridges are examples.
Razors have been sold cheaply as loss leaders to raise demand for the blades.
A perfect complement must be consumed with the other good, like left and right shoes; its indifference curve forms a right angle.
Complementarity need not be mutual: a game needs a console, but a console does not need that game.

definition.text: Substitute goods are goods that can replace each other, so cheaper prices for one reduce demand for the other.

facts.text: Two products with a positive cross elasticity of demand are substitutes.
A perfect substitute can be used in exactly the same way as the good it replaces, and its indifference curves are straight lines.
Someone who sees Coca-Cola and Pepsi Max as perfect substitutes would be happy spending the whole budget on either one.
As a consumer accumulates more of one good, they will pay less for each extra unit of its substitute.
Coca-Cola and Pepsi are close substitutes because both meet the same wish for a cola drink.
When the price of a good rises, demand for its substitutes rises; substitutes have a positive cross elasticity of demand.
Perfect substitutes serve identical uses, so buyers choose purely on price and will not buy the dearer one at all.
Imperfect substitutes are not traded one-for-one because many buyers prefer one brand over the other.

definition.text: Consumer choice theory is the part of microeconomics that explains how people's preferences shape what they spend and how much they demand.

facts.text: It assumes consumers maximise utility subject to their budget constraint, choosing the best bundle they can afford.
Preferences are drawn as indifference curves, each showing bundles that leave the consumer equally satisfied.
Income, culture, product information and psychological factors all affect how consumers value goods.
Every price change splits into an income effect and a substitution effect.
Behavioural economists criticise the theory because consumers often rely on heuristics, rough shortcuts that ignore some information.
People often let sunk costs sway them, like travelling through a storm to use a concert ticket.

title: Income effect

definition.text: The income effect is the change in how much of a good people buy when their real income, or purchasing power, changes.

facts.text: With prices fixed, a change in income shifts the budget line in parallel: outward when income rises, inward when it falls.
A good bought more as income rises is a normal good; one bought less is an inferior good.
Together with the substitution effect, it makes up the full effect of a price change.
When a good gets cheaper, purchasing power rises, so the consumer can buy more of it or of other goods, depending on whether it is a normal or an inferior good.

definition.text: Economists have offered many definitions of their subject, from the study of wealth to the study of choices under scarcity.

facts.text: Economics was first called political economy, stretching the Greek idea of household management to the running of a state.
In 1803 Jean-Baptiste Say defined it as the science of producing, distributing and consuming wealth.
Alfred Marshall in 1890 called it the study of mankind in the ordinary business of life, tied to the material requisites of well-being.
Lionel Robbins in 1932 defined it as the study of human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means with alternative uses, perhaps the most commonly accepted definition today.

definition.text: Diminishing returns is the fall in extra output gained as more of one input is added while all other inputs stay fixed.

facts.text: Also called diminishing marginal productivity, it says that past some point each extra unit of input yields less output.
Output stays positive, but productivity and efficiency fall.
On a factory floor with fixed machines and space, adding workers first more than doubles output, then raises it in proportion, and eventually adds less and less as workers get in each other's way.
Diminishing returns mean rising marginal and average costs, and they explain the bowed-out shape of the production possibilities frontier.
In 1815 Ricardo, Malthus, West and Torrens applied the idea to land rent, drawing on English farming after the Napoleonic Wars.
Technological or managerial innovation can reduce or remove diminishing returns.
Modern versions also hold other outputs equal, since one process can make co-products, such as a factory producing more goods and more CO2.

definition.text: Economic cost is the total value of everything given up for a course of action, including the opportunities passed over.

facts.text: It differs from accounting cost because it includes opportunity cost.
Economists use it to compare how wise one course of action is against another.
Variable costs change with output, while fixed costs come from assets that do not vary with production.
Marginal cost is the extra cost of producing one more unit of output.

definition.text: The economic problem is the set of basic questions every economy must answer: what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom.

facts.text: Economies answer these questions by custom, by central command, or in mixed economies by both market signals and government directives.
Paul Samuelson argued that the price mechanism in competitive markets answers all three questions at once.
Because resources are scarce, producing more of one good means taking resources away from others.
Production is efficient only if no reallocation can make more of one good without making less of another.
Keynes called the struggle for subsistence the most pressing problem not only of humanity but of all life.

definition.text: Equivalent variation is the change in a person's wealth that would affect their well-being as much as a given price change would.

facts.text: John Hicks introduced equivalent and compensating variation in 1939.
Equivalent variation values the welfare change at the old prices, while compensating variation uses the new prices.
It is the most common modern measure of a taxpayer's loss from a distorting tax, and deadweight loss is the gap between it and the tax revenue.

definition.text: The expenditure minimisation problem asks how little money a consumer needs to reach a given level of satisfaction at current prices.

facts.text: It is the mirror image, or dual, of the utility maximisation problem.
The expenditure function gives the minimum money needed, and the Hicksian demand function gives the cheapest bundle that reaches the target.

definition.text: A free good is a good that is not scarce, so it is available in any quantity with no opportunity cost to society.

facts.text: Something given away at zero price is not necessarily a free good, since making it still used scarce resources.
Older textbooks gave seawater and air as examples of goods plentiful enough for everyone to have as much as they want.
Ideas and works that can be copied at almost no cost are free goods, but patents and copyright make some of them scarce to reward their creators.
Treating water as a free good has been blamed for underpricing 98% of water.

definition.text: In economics, goods are things that give someone welfare or satisfaction.

facts.text: Economics studies economic goods, which are scarce because making them takes effort or resources, unlike free goods such as air.
The Earth's atmosphere and seawater are useful but not scarce enough to have a money value.
Final goods are consumed, while intermediate goods, like transistors, are used to make other goods.
Durable goods used to produce further goods, such as machinery, human skills or ecosystems, are capital goods.
Goods are commonly assumed to have diminishing marginal utility.
An elastic good has close substitutes, so a small price change moves demand a lot; an inelastic good, like insulin, has few or none.

definition.text: A bad is the opposite of a good: something with negative value, such as waste, that its owner will pay to be rid of.

facts.text: A bad lowers a consumer's overall welfare.
With a bad, money and the object move the same way, as when a household pays a collector to take away its garbage, giving the garbage a negative price.

definition.text: Economists sort goods into four types by whether people can be kept from using them (excludability) and whether one person's use leaves less for others (rivalry).

facts.text: Private goods such as food and clothing are excludable and rival.
Common-pool resources such as fish stocks and timber are rival but hard to exclude people from, so without clear property rights they may be overfished.
Club goods such as cinemas and cable television are excludable but not rival.
Public goods such as air and national defence are neither excludable nor rival, and mainstream economists accept that markets under-provide them.
In 1977 Elinor and Vincent Ostrom refined the scheme, treating rivalry and excludability as degrees and adding common-pool resources as a fourth type.
Forests, water systems, fisheries and the global atmosphere are common-pool resources vital to human survival.

definition.text: Goods are usually tangible items such as pens or pears, while services are activities other people provide, such as teaching or haircuts.

facts.text: Producing, distributing and consuming goods and services underpins all economic activity and trade.
Most products fall on a continuum between pure goods and pure services: a restaurant sells food and also table service.
Adam Smith counted only work producing material goods as productive and services as unproductive.

definition.text: A Hicksian, or compensated, demand function gives how much of a good a person buys when they keep their satisfaction fixed and spend as little as possible.

facts.text: It shows how demand responds to a price change if income is adjusted to keep the person on the same indifference curve, isolating the substitution effect.
It comes from the expenditure minimisation problem, while Marshallian demand comes from the utility maximisation problem.
Marshallian demand is easier to observe directly, and the two are linked by the Slutsky equation.

definition.text: An implicit cost is the opportunity cost of using something you already own, such as income you could have earned by renting it out or selling it.

facts.text: It is the opposite of an explicit cost, which is paid directly, and it also covers income given up by choosing not to work.
Implicit costs are the gap between economic profit and accounting profit, so economic profit is never more than accounting profit.
A firm on land it bought for $50 a century ago that could rent for $10,000 a month should count the $10,000 as a cost and ignore the $50.

definition.text: An indifference curve is a line on a graph joining all the combinations of two goods that a consumer likes equally well.

facts.text: A set of indifference curves for one person is an indifference map, read like contour lines: curves further out mean more satisfaction.
The slope of an indifference curve is the marginal rate of substitution, the rate at which a consumer will give up one good for more of the other.
Curves are usually bowed toward the origin, and their downward slope expresses a willingness to make trade-offs.
The best affordable choice is where an indifference curve touches the budget line; varying the price traces out a demand curve.
Edgeworth set out the mathematics in 1881, Pareto first drew the curves in 1906, and Hicks and Allen popularised them in the 1930s.
Hovenkamp argued that the endowment effect means people have no indifference curve, so courts should use willingness to accept as the measure of value.

definition.text: An inferior good is one that people buy less of as their income rises.

facts.text: Normal goods are the opposite: demand for them rises with income.
Examples include subcompact economy cars, public transit, payday lending, second-hand clothes and cheap food.
Inferiority reflects affordability, not quality, and the same good can be normal for one group and inferior for another.
Potatoes behave as an inferior good in the Andes but are a high-prestige food in Bangladesh.

title: Giffen good

definition.text: A Giffen good is a rare kind of inferior good that people buy more of when its price rises, breaking the usual law of demand.

facts.text: It must take up so much of a person's spending that a price rise makes them poorer and pushes them to buy even more of it.
The idea is named after Sir Robert Giffen and usually linked to rising potato prices in 19th-century Ireland.
Potatoes were not in fact Giffen goods during the Great Famine in Ireland, and Marshall explained the paradox using bread.
Potatoes in the Irish Great Famine are a classic example: as their price rose, people cut back on meat and vegetables and bought more potatoes.

contested_note: Economists disagree on whether Giffen goods exist in real markets.

title: Margin

definition.text: In economics, the margin is the current level of consumption or production, and marginal concepts describe what happens with one small change in that quantity rather than with the total.

facts.text: Marginal thinking holds that decisions are made one extra unit at a time: whether to get one more unit depends on the benefit of that unit.
Marginal concepts form the basis of price theory and are used to predict the demand for and supply of goods and services.
A firm facing a competitive market price keeps producing until the cost of one more unit would be greater than the sale price.
A consumer keeps buying extra units until the benefit of one more unit equals the market price of that unit.
Neoclassical analysis often assumes goods can be divided endlessly, so a marginal change can be infinitely small; strictly, the smallest relevant division may be quite large.
Economists generally agree that efficient regulation of emissions requires every polluter to face the full marginal social cost of its actions.
Emissions trading lets reductions be made first where the marginal cost of cutting emissions is lowest.

definition.text: The marginal rate of substitution is the rate at which a consumer can give up some of one good for another while staying exactly as satisfied.

facts.text: If the marginal rate of substitution of X for Y is 2, the consumer will give up 2 units of Y to get 1 more unit of X.
Graphically it is the slope (taken as a positive number) of an indifference curve at a given bundle of goods, so it differs at each point on the curve.
It equals the marginal utility of X divided by the marginal utility of Y.
By the law of diminishing marginal rate of substitution, the more of X a consumer has, the less Y they will give up for an extra unit of X.
Utility is maximized when the budget is split so that marginal utility per unit of money spent is equal for every good.
Two people keep trading as long as their marginal rates of substitution differ; when they are equal, no more mutually beneficial exchange is possible.

title: Labour theory of value

definition.text: The labour theory of value holds that a good's economic value is set by the total socially necessary labour needed to produce it.

facts.text: Classical economists such as Adam Smith and David Ricardo used versions of it to explain the long-run 'natural price' of goods; it is usually associated with Marxism.
Smith tied value to the labour a good could command in exchange, while Ricardo tied it to the quantity of labour embodied in making it.
Marx used it to build his theory of surplus value, which holds that profit comes from the unpaid labour of workers taken by capitalists.
In its simplest form, a product's final value is the value of the labour time plus the value of the tools, materials and power used, called constant capital.
From the late 19th century mainstream neoclassical economics largely replaced it with the theory of marginal utility.

contested_note: Critics from the Austrian School and neo-Ricardian economics dispute it, especially over the 'transformation problem' of turning values into prices.

definition.text: Marginalism is the economic theory that explains differences in the value of goods and services by their marginal utility, the extra satisfaction from one more unit.

facts.text: It explains why diamonds cost more than water: water has greater total utility, but a diamond has greater marginal utility.
The law of diminishing marginal utility, also called Gossen's First Law, says each added unit of a good brings less extra benefit than the one before, all else equal.
Marginalism explains prices through supply and demand: buyers want less and sellers offer more as the price rises.
Following Alfred Marshall, marginalists also used marginal physical productivity to explain costs.
At the most general level a marginal cost is a marginal opportunity cost, though it usually means the extra money spent.
Marginalism is an integral part of mainstream economic theory.

title: Marxist criticism of marginalism

definition.text: Marxist economists rejected marginalism, holding to the labour theory of value and arguing that prices cannot be explained by individual preferences alone.

facts.text: Ernest Mandel argued marginalism ignored production and explained at best short-term price swings, not stable long-run prices.
Maurice Dobb argued marginalist prices depend on the distribution of income, since people's ability to express preferences depends on their spending power.
Some economists in the Marxian tradition, such as Oskar Lange and Michał Kalecki, tried to combine it with marginalism and neoclassical economics.

contested_note: Marxist and mainstream economists disagree over whether marginal utility or labour explains value and prices.

definition.text: A Marshallian demand function gives how much of a good a consumer buys as a function of its price, the consumer's income and the prices of other goods.

facts.text: It solves the utility maximization problem: how a consumer gets the most utility from a given income at given prices.
It is also called uncompensated demand, because a price rise is not offset by extra income, unlike the Hicksian demand function; the response mixes a substitution effect and a wealth effect.
If all prices and income rise by the same factor, the quantities bought stay the same.
With strictly convex preferences and positive prices there is a single best bundle, so demand is unique and continuous.

definition.text: Microeconomics is the branch of economics that studies how individuals and firms decide how to use scarce resources, and how they interact.

facts.text: It studies individual markets, sectors and industries, while macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole, such as growth, inflation and unemployment.
One goal is to explain how markets set relative prices and share out limited resources among different uses.
It shows when free markets lead to desirable outcomes and also analyses market failure, when markets fail to produce efficient outcomes.
Its theory usually starts from a single rational individual trying to maximize utility, where rational means having stable, complete and consistent preferences.
It is also called price theory, because prices, set by the actions of buyers and sellers, are central to it.
The micro–macro distinction was likely introduced in 1933 by Ragnar Frisch; the word 'microeconomics' first appeared in print in 1941, from Pieter de Wolff.

title: Fixed and variable costs

definition.text: A fixed cost does not change with how much a firm produces, while a variable cost rises or falls with output.

facts.text: Rent, salaries and utility bills are typical fixed costs; raw materials, delivery and production supplies are typical variable costs.
Over a few months most costs are fixed, but over 10 years most become variable as workers and machines can be changed.
In the short run, total cost equals fixed cost plus total variable cost.

notes: Fixed cost and Variable cost have their own pages in the firms-costs-and-market-structure dossier; this section entry may fold into those.

definition.text: The cost-of-production theory of value says a thing's price is set by the total cost of the resources used to make it.

facts.text: The costs can include any factor of production, such as labour, capital or land, plus taxes.
Adam Smith, its best-known proponent, held that a good's natural price is the sum of wages, profit and rent, while market prices can stray from it in the short term.
The theory works best if returns to scale are constant and there is only one factor of production that is not itself produced.

title: Market structure

definition.text: Market structure describes the features of a market, such as how many firms sell in it, how alike their products are and how easily firms can enter or leave.

facts.text: The market structure determines how prices are formed in that market.
In perfect competition many small firms sell identical products and are price takers, which drives prices down to marginal cost.
In monopolistic competition many firms sell slightly different products, as with restaurants, cereal and clothing.
A monopoly has a single supplier, which tends to charge higher prices and produce below the socially best level.
An oligopoly is dominated by a few firms, which may collude and form cartels that raise prices.
A monopsony has only one buyer, like a mining company that is the only employer in an isolated town and can set wages low.

notes: Belongs more naturally to firms-costs-and-market-structure; Market structure page is crawled but in no dossier.

definition.text: A normal good is one that people buy more of when their income rises, unlike an inferior good, which they buy less of.

facts.text: Whether a good is normal or inferior comes from observation, not from the good itself; the same car can be normal for middle-income buyers and inferior for rich ones.
It is measured by income elasticity of demand: the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income; for a normal good it lies between zero and one.
Luxury goods have an income elasticity greater than one, while necessities have one below one.
When income rises, the demand curve for a normal good shifts outward, so more is wanted at every price.

definition.text: Ordinal utility ranks a person's options in order of preference, saying which is better but not by how much.

facts.text: If George prefers A to B and B to C, any numbers that keep that order describe his preferences equally well; the numbers themselves mean nothing.
All of the theory of consumer choice under certainty can be, and usually is, written in terms of ordinal utility.
Cardinal utility differs by treating the size of the differences between options as meaningful too.
Vilfredo Pareto first introduced the ordinal utility concept in 1906.
Preferences can be drawn as indifference curves; curves further from the origin mean higher utility.
For a utility function to exist, preferences must be complete (any two options can be compared) and transitive (if A beats B and B beats C, A beats C).

title: Positive and normative economics

definition.text: Positive economics describes and explains how the economy works, while normative economics says what people or societies ought to do.

facts.text: A positive statement, such as 'more government spending would lower unemployment', can in principle be checked against evidence.
A normative statement, such as 'milk should cost $6 a gallon so dairy farmers live better', rests on value judgments.
John Neville Keynes defined positive economics as the science of 'what is' and normative economics as the study of 'what ought to be'; his definitions became standard in teaching.
In 1932 Lionel Robbins argued economics should study how to reach given ends with limited resources, not judge which ends to pursue.
Cost–benefit analysis is an example of objective normative analysis: it seeks the best decision given stated assumptions about value.
Ecological economists argue economics is unavoidably normative rather than purely descriptive.

contested_note: Philosophers such as Hilary Putnam dispute that facts and values can be fully separated, and Caplan and Miller argue many supposed value disagreements are really about facts.

definition.text: In economics, a preference is the order in which a person ranks the options open to them, from most to least wanted.

facts.text: Preferences come from taste and need, as opposed to price, availability or income.
Transitivity, preferring A to C whenever one prefers A to B and B to C, is a basic principle shared by most models of decision-making.
A preference order that is both transitive and complete is called rational, and people who follow one are called rational agents.
Real preferences are not always transitive, because people are not always rational and preferences can form cycles with no best choice.
Most economic models assume stable preferences, an assumption long disputed outside neoclassical economics.
Preferences can change through new technology and social influence, as when friends at lunch shift each other's food choices.
In 1926 Ragnar Frisch first built a mathematical model of preferences for demand and utility theory.

title: Convex preferences

definition.text: Convex preferences are preferences in which averages are liked better than extremes, so a person prefers a mix of goods to a lot of just one.

facts.text: The idea roughly matches diminishing marginal utility without needing a utility function.
With strictly convex preferences, the average of two equally liked bundles is preferred to either, so indifference curves bow in toward the origin.
Perfect substitutes give straight-line indifference curves, where the average gives the same utility.

notes: Page crawled but in no chapter dossier.

definition.text: A production-possibility frontier is a graph showing every combination of two outputs an economy can make when all its resources are used fully and efficiently.

facts.text: It illustrates scarcity, opportunity cost and efficiency: one good can only be made by moving resources away from, and making less of, another.
A point on the curve is efficient, a point inside it means resources are wasted or idle, and a point beyond it is impossible with current resources and technology.
The frontier shifts outward when inputs such as labour or capital grow or technology improves, which is economic growth.
It shifts inward if the labour force shrinks, raw materials are depleted, or a natural, military or ecological disaster destroys productive capacity.
It is usually drawn bowed outward because opportunity cost rises: resources less suited to a good are moved into it as its output grows.
In one example, 10 more packets of butter cost 5 guns when little butter is made, but 50 guns when butter output is already near its maximum.
An economy can be productively efficient without being allocatively efficient: market failures such as externalities can lead it to produce the wrong mix of goods.

definition.text: The marginal rate of transformation is the slope of the production-possibility frontier: how much of one good must be given up to make one more unit of another.

facts.text: It is also called the marginal opportunity cost of a good in terms of the other.
If the slope at a point is 2, producing one more packet of butter means giving up 2 guns.
Pareto efficiency is reached when the marginal rate of transformation equals every consumer's marginal rate of substitution.

definition.text: The Slutsky equation splits the change in demand caused by a price change into a substitution effect and an income effect.

facts.text: It links ordinary (Marshallian) demand to compensated (Hicksian) demand, which holds the consumer's utility fixed.
The substitution effect is always negative because indifference curves slope downward; the sign of the income effect depends on the good.
Since utility cannot be observed, the substitution effect cannot be seen directly but can be calculated from the two observable terms.
It explains why the law of demand fails for Giffen goods, where a strong income effect outweighs the substitution effect.

title: Subjective theory of value

definition.text: The subjective theory of value holds that a good's value is set by the people buying or selling it, not by any property of the good or the labour that went into it.

facts.text: It is usually contrasted with the labour theory of value, from which it broke away during the marginal revolution.
Jevons, Walras and Menger created its modern version independently and almost at the same time in the late 19th century.
A good's value can change after it is made, with age, personal attachment, cultural meaning or scarcity, as with collectable cars and comic books.
Because trades are voluntary, both sides value what they receive more than what they give, so trade itself can create value.
It helps explain why non-essential goods can be worth more than essential ones.
Alfred Marshall combined both views: prices depend on objective production costs (supply) and consumers' subjective utility (demand).

notes: Lead claim S:28792d060d7d is tagged 'according to whom?'.

definition.text: The substitution effect is the change in what a consumer buys caused purely by a change in the relative prices of goods, as they switch toward the one that became cheaper.

facts.text: Any price change can be split into a substitution effect and an income effect, which comes from the change in purchasing power.
On a graph, the substitution effect is a move along the original indifference curve, and the income effect is the move to a different curve.
John Hicks and R. G. D. Allen introduced the idea to English readers in 1934, building on Pareto and reaching conclusions Eugen Slutsky had found in 1915.
The related elasticity of substitution, defined by Hicks and by Joan Robinson, measures how the mix of inputs used shifts as their relative prices change.

definition.text: A sunk cost is money, time or effort already spent that cannot be recovered.

facts.text: It contrasts with prospective costs, future costs that can still be avoided by acting.
Standard economic theory holds that only future costs matter to a rational decision; this is called the bygones principle or marginal principle.

A factory expected to cost $100 million and yield $120 million should be abandoned if, after $30 million is spent, its value projection falls to $65 million, since finishing would cost $70 million more.
If the projection instead falls to $75 million, a rational company should continue the project.
In everyday life people often let past spending, for example on repairing a car or house, shape their future decisions.

definition.text: The sunk cost fallacy is the tendency to keep going with something because of what has already been invested in it, even when stopping would be better.

facts.text: It is described as 'throwing good money after bad' instead of 'cutting one's losses'.
Managers of many US utility companies were found to be overly reluctant to end economically unviable nuclear plant projects.
Behavioural economics links it to framing effects, overoptimism, a sense of personal responsibility and the wish not to appear wasteful.
In one study, managers told they had made an earlier poor investment put in an average of $12.97 million more, versus $9.43 million for those told someone else had.

definition.text: The utility maximization problem describes how a consumer chooses the most preferred bundle of goods they can afford with limited income at given prices.

facts.text: It assumes the consumer can rank every possible bundle by the utility it gives.
It gives a systematic account of consumer demand and how it changes when income or prices change.
The constraint reflects scarcity; besides money, consumers may face time constraints and budgets spread over time.
If all prices and income rise at the same rate, the affordable set and the best choice stay the same.
Because of bounded rationality, such as lack of time or information, real consumers sometimes pick bundles that do not maximize utility.
The problem was first developed by the utilitarian philosophers Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill.

definition.text: Absolute advantage is the ability of a person, firm or country to produce a good or service more efficiently than others.

facts.text: Adam Smith first described it in The Wealth of Nations in 1776, arguing against mercantilism that all nations could gain from free trade and specialization.
If the UK needs fewer hours to make cloth and Portugal fewer to make wine, specializing and trading leaves both with more of each good.
A party can have no absolute advantage in anything yet still gain from trade through comparative advantage.

definition.text: An economic model is a simplified, often mathematical, picture of an economic process, built from a set of variables and the relationships between them.

facts.text: Simplifying matters because economies are shaped by many things at once, including decisions, resource limits, environmental and geographical constraints, laws and chance.
Models are used to forecast economic activity, propose and justify policy, and plan in firms and centrally planned economies.
Some models only predict the direction of change, such as demand falling when a price rises, and are often drawn as two-dimensional graphs.
Most models rest on unrealistic assumptions, such as perfect information or frictionless markets, and may leave out important issues such as externalities.
In the late 1980s the Brookings Institution compared 12 leading macroeconomic models and found they gave significantly different answers to the same shocks.
Like weather forecasts, economic forecasts fail because models cannot capture full detail and are sensitive to small changes in their equations.

definition.text: An economic system is the way a society organizes the production, allocation and distribution of goods and services.

facts.text: Every economic system must answer basic questions forced by scarcity: what to produce, how to produce it and who gets what is produced.
Systems are usually classed by who owns the means of production and by how resources are allocated, through markets or planning.
Private ownership with markets is called market capitalism; public or cooperative ownership with planning is a socialist planned economy; public ownership with markets is market socialism.
By allocation mechanism, systems include market, mixed, planned, traditional, subsistence and gift economies.
Capitalism features private ownership of the means of production and a market economy for coordination.
By the 1990s most communist states had ended or reformed their centrally planned economies toward markets.

title: Mixed economy

definition.text: A mixed economy combines features of capitalism, such as private businesses, with features of socialism, such as government-run services.

facts.text: It can mean blending markets with planning, markets with state intervention, or private with public enterprise.

In the version advocated by John Maynard Keynes, private ownership and profit-seeking remain dominant, but markets are regulated and governments use fiscal and monetary policy to fight booms, busts, unemployment and inequality.
Governments in such economies provide public goods and services such as education, healthcare, infrastructure, environmental protection and management of public lands.
Most market-oriented economies today, including the United States, fall in this category, as do the Nordic countries with their extensive welfare states.
China, Norway, Singapore and Vietnam have large state-owned enterprise sectors alongside large private sectors.
Because real economies rarely match an ideal, mixed economies are usually described as leaning toward either private or public ownership.

contested_note: Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek and orthodox Marxists argue there can be no lasting mixture of capitalism and socialism, since either markets or planning must drive the economy.

title: Neoclassical economics

definition.text: Neoclassical economics is the approach that explains production, consumption and prices through supply and demand, driven by people maximizing utility and firms maximizing profit.

facts.text: It rests on three assumptions: people have rational preferences, individuals maximize utility and firms maximize profits, and people act independently with full information.
It holds that a good's value comes from its marginal utility to the user, unlike classical and Marxian economics, which use the labour theory of value.
It is the dominant approach to microeconomics; combined with Keynesian economics it formed the neoclassical synthesis that dominated mainstream economics from the 1950s.
Although it favours markets, it accepts that externalities, a form of market failure, can stop markets from producing socially desirable outcomes.
Under suitable assumptions, flexible prices allow all welfare-improving trades, so free markets yield an optimum of social welfare.
Thorstein Veblen coined the term in 1900; its shift from classical economics is often dated to Jevons and Menger (1871) and Walras (1874–1877).
In this view a good's value comes from individuals maximizing their satisfaction within their incomes and firms maximizing profit given their costs.
It developed in the 1870s and replaced classical economics as the mainstream, also in the English-speaking world.

notes: Drafted from the history chapter; likely also an entry in an economics-basics chapter, so merge there if one exists.

title: Criticisms of neoclassical economics

definition.text: Many economists and other schools of thought criticize neoclassical economics, especially its assumptions about rational, self-interested, fully informed people.

facts.text: Marxist, behavioural, Austrian, post-Keynesian, institutionalist and other schools each differ from the neoclassical school; insiders such as Joseph Stiglitz also criticize it.
Veblen mocked its picture of a person as 'a lightning calculator of pleasures and pains'; behavioural economists study how real decisions differ from its assumptions.
Hayek argued that by assuming full information, its equilibrium models assume away the real problem of discovering knowledge spread among many people.
It is often accused of a normative bias despite claiming to be value-free, and critics call for more pluralistic teaching.
Critics say it promotes commodification and privatization because it holds that market exchange usually allocates goods best.
Defenders note it is also the main tool for assessing how policies affect inequality.

contested_note: Schools disagree over whether neoclassical assumptions and mathematical methods are sound, and whether modern mainstream models have moved beyond neoclassical economics.

title: Economic value

definition.text: Economic value is a measure of the benefit a good or service gives to a person, firm or other economic agent.

facts.text: It is usually measured in money, as the most a person is willing and able to pay for a good or service.
Value is how much of one wanted thing a person would give up to get another.
Early economists split value into value in use and value in exchange; value links to price through exchange.
Rival schools hold different theories of value: the labour theory ties it to labour needed for production, while the subjective theory ties it to buyers' marginal utility.
Many neoclassical theories equate value with market price, so something with no market to set a price has no economic value.
Biodiversity is increasingly seen as having economic value because of ecosystem services such as clean air, food, water, flood defence and pollination.

contested_note: Different schools of economics disagree about what determines value, and value theories are a major source of their disagreements.
notes: Titled 'Economic value' to avoid clashing with ethics pages on value; article is Value (economics).

title: Institutional economics

definition.text: Institutional economics studies how institutions, such as firms, states, laws and social norms, and their evolution shape economic behaviour.

facts.text: It sees markets as the result of complex interactions between institutions rather than as given.
It focuses on learning, bounded rationality and evolution instead of assuming stable preferences, rationality and equilibrium.
Its name traces to a 1919 article by Walton H. Hamilton, and it was central to American economics in the early 20th century through Thorstein Veblen, Wesley Mitchell and John R. Commons.
Veblen's The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899) analysed how people consume conspicuously to display success.
New institutional economics tried to bring institutionalism into mainstream economics through theories of property rights, information and transaction costs.
The older tradition continues today as a leading heterodox approach.

notes: Critics say 'institution' is so vague that who counts as an institutionalist is endlessly disputed (S:d92bb9341732).
